title: Modi Calls for Global Framework to Fight Cyber Fraud, Deepfakes
excerpt: At the India Mobile Congress 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged governments, tech firms, telcos and banks to build a shared mechanism that stops digital fraud before it reaches people — and offered India's hard-won expertise.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi, inaugurating the 10th India Mobile Congress in New Delhi on October 8, called for a global mechanism — involving governments, tech companies, telecom operators and financial institutions — to stop cyber fraud and deepfakes before they reach victims.
  • The pitch builds on his October 6 meeting with the GSMA board, where he pressed for common global standards on emerging technology and clear identification of AI-generated and deepfake content.
  • The scale of the problem at home: Indians lost ₹3,588.2 crore across more than 5.83 lakh digital payment fraud cases between FY22 and September FY26. In 2025, nearly 7.1% of attempted digital transactions in India were suspected fraud — almost double the 3.8% global rate.
  • What this means for you: digital fraud disproportionately targets families in India, including elderly parents of NRIs who receive scam calls from overseas numbers. A cross-border mechanism would make it easier to trace fraudsters operating from other countries. If you support family in India, register them on the Sanchar Saathi portal to report suspected fraud communications, and save the National Cybercrime Helpline 1930.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday called for a global framework to tackle cyber frauds, deepfakes and digital crimes, saying digital threats have crossed national boundaries and require coordinated action by all stakeholders. Inaugurating the tenth edition of the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi, themed "Scale Without Boundaries," Modi said governments, technology companies, telecom operators and financial institutions must jointly build mechanisms to curb digital fraud.

"I urge the GSMA and telecom operators across the world: come, let us create a global mechanism that can stop such fraud before it reaches the people."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of India

"A person sitting in one country, with the help of a person in another country, can commit a crime in a third country," Modi said, describing how most fraud operations are inherently borderless. Deepfakes, he added, have become one of the biggest challenges facing the digital world. "Technology can achieve scale only when it gains people's trust," he said.

Context & Background

Modi's remarks at the IMC follow his October 6 interaction with the board of the GSMA — the global industry body representing mobile operators — at Seva Teerth in New Delhi. According to the Press Information Bureau, Modi told the board that cyber fraud requires technology-driven solutions, suggested sustained awareness messages warning users about fraudulent calls, and called for global standards for emerging technologies along with clear identification of AI-generated and deepfake content. In a post on X after the meeting, he wrote that the digital future "must expand opportunity while strengthening trust."

India has also moved on provenance at home. February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules require platforms offering AI content tools to embed permanent metadata or other provenance mechanisms in synthetic content "to the extent technically feasible," including a unique identifier for the platform tool used to create or alter it — and forbid users from removing it.

The call also fits India's positioning of its Digital Public Infrastructure as a model for the Global South. At the GSMA meeting, Modi described DPI as a "springboard" for developing countries and stressed affordable access and technology for the last mile.

Impact & Analysis

India is fighting one of the world's most intense digital-fraud battles, making the appeal more than rhetoric. Beyond the ₹3,588.2 crore in reported losses, the government's Sanchar Saathi portal has received 12.8 lakh inputs on suspected fraud communications since its 2023 launch, and the Financial Fraud Risk Indicator has helped prevent more than ₹5,000 crore in suspected cyber-fraud losses, according to government figures cited this week.

The policy response is also widening: Home Minister Amit Shah has directed officials to upgrade the National Cybercrime Helpline with AI to make reporting easier and to fix problems around bank accounts frozen during fraud investigations, while the RBI has introduced a compensation mechanism under which the Centre and banks shoulder part of unrecovered losses — customers losing up to ₹50,000 can claim up to 85% of the net loss or ₹25,000, whichever is lower.

A global mechanism of the kind Modi describes would be genuinely difficult to build: it would need real-time intelligence sharing across telcos, banks and law enforcement in dozens of jurisdictions, plus agreement on standards for caller authentication and deepfake detection. India's pitch carries weight precisely because of its experience — it has one of the world's largest UPI transaction volumes and, with it, one of the largest fraud surfaces.

Diaspora Angle

The Indian diaspora is on both sides of this fraud economy. Scam call centers targeting Indians in the US, UK and Canada increasingly operate across borders, while elderly relatives in India are prime targets for "digital arrest" scams and fake investment pitches run from overseas. Any credible cross-border fraud-tracing mechanism would directly reduce the harm reaching diaspora households.

What's Next

Telecom Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia used the same IMC stage to announce that India will take its 5G user base from 550 million to one billion by 2030, declaring that a country once behind the world in 4G is resolved to lead in 6G. The tenth IMC's discussions, Modi said, will create a roadmap for the next decade of telecom in India and globally. Whether the global fraud mechanism moves from exhortation to architecture will depend on whether the GSMA, governments and banks pick up the proposal in the months ahead.
